items.title: Go Turns 17
items.author: Austin Clements, for the Go team
items.content:
Over the past year, we released Go 1.26 in February and Go 1.27 in August, alongside a steady stream of releases across our libraries and developer tools. Meanwhile, the pace of change across the software industry continues to accelerate, driven by shifting hardware, evolving security threats, and the rapid rise of AI-assisted development and agentic systems.

In a tumultuous time for the industry, Go aims to be a steady hand on the tiller. Our goal is to keep Go grounded in its foundational principles of simplicity, reliability, efficiency, and an unwavering commitment to compatibility, while adapting to modern hardware, production workloads, and developer workflows. Increasingly, our investments serve a : what helps human engineers write, understand, and maintain reliable Go code at scale also provides the guardrails and authoritative context that AI coding assistants and agents need to be effective.

Core language and library improvements

In the language itself, Go 1.26 and 1.27 addressed several long-standing restrictions in generics and everyday Go syntax, guided by years of real-world experience. When generics first landed in Go 1.18, methods could not declare their own type parameters, which sometimes forced awkward package-level functions and “inside-out” nested calls. Go 1.27 introduced generic methods on non-interface types (such as the new method in ), allowing APIs to stay naturally organized on types and enabling readable method chaining. Together with support for self-referential type constraints in Go 1.26 and broader type inference for generic function values in Go 1.27, generics in Go feel more complete and natural than ever.

Alongside generics, two refinements to value construction make everyday Go code cleaner and more concise. Go 1.26 extended the built-in function to accept an initial value expression, allowing or without the ubiquitous -style helper functions used to populate optional pointer fields in JSON and protocol buffer structs. And in Go 1.27, struct literal keys can refer directly to fields of embedded or nested structs, reducing boilerplate in composite literals.

In the standard library, our focus has been on evolving Go’s “production stack” and eliminating subtle operational traps. Few packages are as central to that as , which has been a mainstay of Go since before Go 1.0. While its core model has held up remarkably well for over 15 years, tighter JSON standards and security expectations have turned some of its original defaults into interoperability and security hazards, such as silently accepting invalid UTF-8 or duplicate object keys and matching struct fields case-insensitively. At the same time, its buffered design prevented true streaming and limited performance. Addressing these issues while upholding Go’s compatibility promise for the millions of existing programs that depend on meant designing a new major version of the package.

Six years in the making, the new and packages reached general availability in Go 1.27. Driven by Joe Tsai, Daniel Martí, and contributors from across the Go community, this modern JSON API brings safer, stricter defaults, flexible caller- and type-specified customization, and up to 10× faster unmarshaling, while cleanly separating high-level semantic marshaling () from low-level, reflection-free syntactic streaming (). Crucially, we didn’t leave existing code behind: the original package is now implemented entirely in terms of under the hood. Existing callers get faster unmarshaling simply by upgrading, and packages using and interoperate seamlessly so that the ecosystem can migrate gradually without flag days.

We’ve also brought new production diagnostics to Go’s concurrency primitives. Concurrency is one of Go’s greatest strengths, but goroutines accidentally left blocked on abandoned channels or locks can silently leak memory and CPU in long-running services, and traditional goroutine profiles cannot distinguish leaked goroutines from ones legitimately waiting for work. First previewed in Go 1.26 and now generally available in Go 1.27, the new goroutine leak profiler ( in and /debug/pprof/goroutineleak in ) solves this for production services. Contributed by Vlad Saioc and Uber’s Programming Systems team, building on academic research with Aarhus University and Washington University in St. Louis, the profiler repurposes the garbage collector’s reachability phase to identify goroutines blocked on concurrency primitives that no runnable goroutine can ever reach. That allows it to pinpoint leaks in production with near-zero false positives and zero overhead when not in use.

In , closing an HTTP/1 response body with even a single unread byte—such as a trailing newline left behind by a JSON decoder—previously forced the client to tear down the underlying TCP and TLS connection. Go 1.27’s HTTP transport now automatically drains small unread response bodies in the background on close, turning a widespread latency footgun into up to a 5× speedup for sequential HTTP/1 requests while letting application code stay clean and simple.

These releases also added several notable standard library APIs, including a native package, a generic and type-safe , and an in-memory designed for virtual-time testing with . Existing packages saw significant speedups as well: now runs twice as fast while allocating half as much memory, compresses faster (speeding up , , , and ), and has a faster, more accurate encoder and decoder.

Making the most of modern hardware

Modern CPUs look very different from the hardware Go first launched on 17 years ago, with wide vector units and deep, non-uniform memory hierarchies. A major focus of our runtime and compiler work is ensuring Go programs make full use of modern silicon, both transparently when you upgrade your toolchain and through new APIs when you need explicit control.

After debuting as an experiment in Go 1.25, the Green Tea garbage collector became the default in Go 1.26. By organizing object marking around contiguous memory spans rather than chasing pointers across the heap, Green Tea aligns with modern CPU memory architectures to reduce garbage collection overhead by 10–40% in real-world workloads—and by an additional ~10% on recent processors using AVX-512 vector instructions during scanning.

Of course, the runtime shouldn’t be the only part of a Go program that can tap into vector hardware. Without access to Single Instruction, Multiple Data (SIMD) capabilities, compute-intensive software, from cryptography and media processing to data analytics and AI, leaves a significant portion of modern silicon dark. Until recently, the only way to light up that hardware in Go was by writing and maintaining per-architecture assembly. To change that, Go 1.26 and 1.27 introduced two experimental SIMD packages: , for low-level access to architecture-specific vector instructions on , (NEON), and WebAssembly (); and , a higher-level, width-agnostic API that provides portable, near-assembly performance across architectures with automatic fallback emulation.

We’ve also attacked the cost of memory allocation from multiple angles. The cheapest heap allocation is the one that never happens: in Go 1.26, the compiler began allocating initial slice backing stores on the stack at sites—even for slices that ultimately escape to the heap—eliminating the flurry of small heap allocations that typically accompany slice growth. And for heap allocations more broadly, Go 1.27 introduced size-specialized memory allocation to speed up allocating the small objects (such as small structs, slices, and strings) that dominate allocator time. Generating dedicated fast-path allocator routines for size classes up to 80 bytes made small allocations up to 30% faster and improved overall performance in allocation-heavy programs. Together with a ~30% reduction in baseline call overhead in Go 1.26, these improvements make Go programs faster and leaner out of the box.

Secure software and ecosystem defense

Go’s approach to security spans the entire lifecycle of software: providing safe APIs by design, preparing cryptography for the future, and actively defending the live ecosystem as new threats emerge.

To defend against store-now, decrypt-later attacks and support the industry’s accelerating timelines for quantum readiness, Go has continued expanding its post-quantum cryptography support. Go 1.26 enabled hybrid post-quantum key exchanges ( and ) by default in and added the package (implementing RFC 9180 Hybrid Public Key Encryption, including post-quantum hybrid KEMs). Go 1.27 followed up with the new package, implementing the FIPS 204 post-quantum ML-DSA signature standard and integrating it into and .

At the same time, we’ve continued hardening the standard library and runtime against subtle classes of vulnerabilities. Most key generation and signing functions across Go’s packages now unconditionally draw from a secure system randomness source, closing off a classic footgun where non-cryptographic readers were accidentally passed in. Under the hood, Go 1.26 also added 64-bit heap base address randomization to harden binaries and introduced the experimental package for eagerly erasing sensitive cryptographic temporaries from registers, stack frames, and the heap.

Securing Go deployments also requires rapid vulnerability and incident response in a fast-moving threat landscape. From the Go vulnerability database and to our release infrastructure, we’ve invested heavily in ecosystem defense. In October, that preparation was put to the test during the eMudhra certificate key disclosure incident, when eight intermediate TLS and code-signing certificates chaining to a widely trusted root CA were discovered to use trivially weak private keys. Because Linux lacks a uniform OS-level certificate revocation mechanism, Go’s built-in TLS verifier is the frontline defense for millions of Linux services. Within seven and a half hours of initial notification, the Go Security team shipped a targeted block in our first-ever URGENT track security release (Go 1.27.3 and Go 1.26.10) alongside an updated Go vulnerability database entry so could flag affected binaries, giving Go users everything they needed to protect their deployments before the weak keys were publicly disclosed the next morning.

Go has always been more than a compiler and standard library: it is an end-to-end platform for software engineering. Over the past year, our work in , the language server, , and has focused on making that platform even more productive for both human developers and AI coding assistants.

In last fall’s Go Developer Survey, the single biggest challenge developers reported was ensuring their code follows best practices and current Go idioms. As Go evolves while standing by its compatibility promise, older ways of writing code continue to work alongside newer, clearer, or faster alternatives, creating a natural drift in idioms over time. That drift has been compounded by AI coding assistants, which gravitate toward the older patterns that dominate their training data.

Go 1.26 tackled this with a complete overhaul of the command, returning the long-dormant tool to its pre-Go 1.0 roots to apply dozens of automatic across entire codebases. What did for stylistic consistency, modernizers aim to do for idiomatic consistency. Available both as instant suggestions in and as bulk, push-button upgrades in , modernizers simplify existing code and help developers discover new language and library features. We now routinely consider whether new language and library proposals should ship with a modernizer of their own. Just as importantly, modernizers give coding agents an immediate way to bring generated code up to date, while helping shift the global corpus of open source Go code so that future models learn modern idioms from the start.

Bespoke modernizers work well for the language and standard library, but a centralized team can never write them for every third-party module in the ecosystem. That’s why Go 1.26 also introduced the annotation-driven source-level inliner, the first step toward a “self-service” paradigm for automated code maintenance. Any package author can now annotate a deprecated function, type, or constant with , and the inliner will safely migrate callers and references via or in the IDE, carefully handling evaluation order, side effects, and name shadowing.

In the editor, we’ve made four feature-packed releases of over the past year (v0.21.0, v0.22.0, v0.23.0, and v0.24.0). In collaboration with the Dart team, we designed and proposed an open Language Server Protocol (LSP) extension for interactive refactoring, allowing language servers to ask for user input through dynamic, multi-step dialogs in any supporting editor. Now integrated into and , interactive refactoring powers customizable struct tag addition and removal, interface implementation (including generic interfaces) with live symbol search, and cross-package declaration moves. Beyond refactoring, also gained generalized package renaming across directories, zero-configuration support for editing Go assembly files, subexpression hover inspection, completions and inlay hints for promoted fields, automatic scanning when dependencies change, and continued enhancements to its built-in Model Context Protocol (MCP) server for AI coding assistants.

Rounding out the developer platform, in May we launched the official API and followed up with support for in Go 1.27. Previously, developer tools and IDE integrations had to resort to fragile web scraping to query ecosystem metadata. Today, the API gives tool authors and AI coding agents a fast, authoritative service for querying module versions, package symbols, importers, and vulnerability data, while makes it easy to pull up documentation for any version of any package right from the command line.

We have an ambitious year ahead for Go.

On the tooling front, we’re building on the API, , and to make Go’s developer tools even more capable for both human developers and coding agents. Following the strong community response to and , we’re exploring ways to expand self-service static analysis, enabling developers, package maintainers, and organizations to easily integrate custom analyzers and domain-specific best-practice checks directly into their development workflows. We’re also exploring ways to surface richer package health and quality signals on and through its API, helping developers and coding agents evaluate and choose trustworthy, reliable dependencies.

In the language and libraries, Go 1.28 will resolve one of Go’s longest-standing language requests by allowing composite literals to omit redundant types whenever the type can be inferred from context, cutting visual noise in deeply nested configurations, API requests, and table-driven tests. And with recent generics refinements and hashing APIs in place, we’ve just accepted a swath of proposals for generic collection APIs—including sets, ordered maps, and more—which will land in over the next few weeks so the community can try them out and share feedback ahead of future standard library inclusion.

Under the hood, we’re working hard to graduate a large subset of the and packages (covering , NEON, and ) in Go 1.28, with further expansions and scalable vector (SVE) support targeted for Go 1.29. Amid the global RAM crunch, reducing Go’s memory footprint is also one of our major priorities for the coming year.

Finally, ensuring Go stands the test of time means scaling not just our technology, but the open source project itself. Over the past year, some of Go’s most impactful advances, including and the profile, were driven by or built in close partnership with contributors outside Google. To better support our growing ecosystem and contributor base, we’re working to bridge the gap between Go maintainers at Google and our broader community, and to diversify Go’s technical stewardship. That includes restructuring the proposal process to improve throughput, give the community clearer visibility into the process and input into prioritization, and formally involve community contributors in triage and review. Beyond proposals, we are building a clearer contributor ladder to empower proven contributors with greater autonomy, decision-making privileges, and maintenance responsibilities, and opening up maintainer summits and day-to-day communications to trusted contributors from our amazing community.

Seventeen years in, Go is thriving because of the people who use it, build with it, and contribute to it every day. Thank you to everyone in the Go community for being part of this journey, and we wish you all the best in the year ahead!

items.title: A new Go API for JSON
items.author: Michael Pratt, Joe Tsai, Daniel Martí, Johan Brandhorst-Satzkorn, Roger Peppe, Chris Hines, and Damien Neil
items.content:
JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) is a simple data interchange format, the most popular data format used on the internet, and widely read and written by Go programs. Go has included support for JSON in the standard library since well before Go 1.0. We first wrote about support for JSON in Go more than 15 years ago!

Over time, packages evolve with the needs of their users, and is no exception. Last year, we wrote about a new experimental API for JSON designed to bring long-awaited improvements and fixes.

After additional feedback and refinement, the new and packages are stable and generally available in Go 1.27! This post is an updated version of the article introducing the experiment, describing the problems with and introducing the new packages.

Problems with

Overall, has held up well. The idea of marshaling and unmarshaling arbitrary Go types with some default representation in JSON, combined with the ability to customize the representation, has proven to be highly flexible. However, in the years since its introduction, various users have identified numerous shortcomings.

There are various behavioral flaws in :

  • Imprecise handling of JSON syntax: Over the years, JSON has seen increased standardization in order for programs to properly communicate. Generally, decoders have become stricter at rejecting ambiguous inputs, to reduce the chance that two implementations will have different (successful) interpretations of a particular JSON value.

    • currently accepts invalid UTF-8, whereas the latest Internet Standard (RFC 8259) requires valid UTF-8. The default behavior should report an error in the presence of invalid UTF-8, instead of introducing silent data corruption, which may cause problems downstream.

    • currently accepts objects with duplicate member names. RFC 8259 does not specify how to handle duplicate names, so an implementation is free to choose an arbitrary value, merge the values, discard the values, or report an error. The presence of a duplicate name results in a JSON value without a universally agreed upon meaning. This could be exploited by attackers in security applications and has been exploited before (as in CVE-2017-12635). The default behavior should err on the side of safety and reject duplicate names.

  • Leaking nilness of slices and maps: JSON is often used to communicate with programs using JSON implementations that do not allow to be unmarshaled into a data type expected to be a JSON array or object. Since marshals a nil slice or map as a JSON , this may lead to errors when unmarshaling by other implementations. A survey indicated that most Go users prefer that nil slices and maps are marshaled as an empty JSON array or object by default.

  • Case-insensitive unmarshaling: When unmarshaling, a JSON object member name is resolved to a Go struct field name using a case-insensitive match. This is a surprising default, a potential security vulnerability, and a performance limitation.

  • Inconsistent calling of methods: Due to an implementation detail, methods declared on a pointer receiver are inconsistently called by . While regarded as a bug, this cannot be fixed as too many applications depend on the current behavior.

The API of can be tricky or restrictive:

  • It is difficult to correctly unmarshal from an . Users often write json.NewDecoder(r).Decode(v), which fails to reject trailing junk at the end of the input.

  • Options can be set on the and types, but cannot be used with the and functions. Similarly, types implementing the and interfaces cannot make use of the options and there is no way to plumb options down the call stack. For example, the Decoder.DisallowUnknownFields option loses its effect when calling a custom method.

  • The , , and functions write to a instead of something more flexible like a or . This limits the usability of those functions.

Setting aside internal implementation details, the public API commits it to certain performance limitations:

  • : The interface method forces the implementation to allocate the returned . Also, the semantics require that verify that the result is valid JSON and also to reformat it to match the specified indentation.

  • : The interface method requires that a complete JSON value be provided (without any trailing data). This forces to parse the JSON value to be unmarshaled in its entirety to determine where it ends before it can call . Afterwards, the method itself must parse the provided JSON value again.

  • : Even though the and types operate on an or , they buffer the entire JSON value in memory. The method for reading individual tokens is allocation-heavy and there is no corresponding API for writing tokens.

Furthermore, if the implementation of a or method recursively calls the or function, then the performance becomes quadratic.

Trying to fix directly

Introducing a new, incompatible major version of a package is a heavy consideration. If possible, we should try to fix the existing package.

While it is relatively easy to add new features, it is difficult to change existing features. Unfortunately, these problems are inherent consequences of the existing API, making them practically impossible to fix within the Go 1 compatibility promise.

We could in principle declare separate names, such as or , but that is tantamount to creating a parallel namespace within the same package. This leads us to (henceforth called ), where we can make these changes within a separate namespace in contrast to (henceforth called ).

Building on

Before discussing the API, we first introduce the package that lays the foundation for improvements to JSON in Go.

JSON serialization in Go can be broken down into two primary components:

  • that is concerned with processing JSON based on its grammar, and
  • that defines the relationship between JSON values and Go values.

We use the terms “encode” and “decode” to describe syntactic functionality and the terms “marshal” and “unmarshal” to describe semantic functionality. We aim to provide a clear distinction between functionality that is purely concerned with encoding versus that of marshaling.

This diagram provides an overview of this separation. Purple blocks represent types, while blue blocks represent functions or methods. The direction of the arrows approximately represents the flow of data. The bottom half of the diagram, implemented by the package, contains functionality that is only concerned with syntax, while the upper half, implemented by the package, contains functionality that assigns semantic meaning to syntactic data handled by the bottom half.

The basic API of is the following:

package jsontext

type Encoder struct { ... }
func NewEncoder(io.Writer, ...Options) *Encoder
func (*Encoder) WriteValue(Value) error
func (*Encoder) WriteToken(Token) error

type Decoder struct { ... }
func NewDecoder(io.Reader, ...Options) *Decoder
func (*Decoder) ReadValue() (Value, error)
func (*Decoder) ReadToken() (Token, error)

type Kind byte
type Value []byte
func (Value) Kind() Kind
type Token struct { ... }
func (Token) Kind() Kind

The package provides functionality for interacting with JSON at a syntactic level and derives its name from RFC 8259, section 2 where the grammar for JSON data is literally called . Since it only interacts with JSON at a syntactic level, it does not depend on Go reflection.

The and provide support for encoding and decoding JSON values and tokens. The constructors accept variadic options that affect the particular behavior of encoding and decoding. Unlike the and types declared in , the new types in avoid muddling the distinction between syntax and semantics and operate in a truly streaming manner.

A JSON value is a complete unit of data and is represented in Go as a named . It is identical to in , which is now a type alias to . A JSON value is syntactically composed of one or more JSON tokens. A JSON token is represented in Go as the opaque type with constructors and accessor methods. It is analogous to in but is designed to represent arbitrary JSON tokens without allocation.

To resolve the fundamental performance problems with the and interface methods, we need an efficient way of encoding and decoding JSON as a streaming sequence of tokens and values. In , we introduce the and interface methods that operate on an or , allowing the methods’ implementations to process JSON in a purely streaming manner. Thus, the package need not be responsible for validating or formatting a JSON value returned by , nor would it need to be responsible for determining the boundaries of a JSON value provided to . These responsibilities belong to the and .

Introducing

Building on the package, we now introduce the package. It is designed to fix the problems in , while remaining familiar to users of the package. Our goal is that usages of will operate the same if directly migrated to .

The basic API of is the following:

package json

func Marshal(in any, opts ...Options) (out []byte, err error)
func MarshalWrite(out io.Writer, in any, opts ...Options) error
func MarshalEncode(out *jsontext.Encoder, in any, opts ...Options) error

func Unmarshal(in []byte, out any, opts ...Options) error
func UnmarshalRead(in io.Reader, out any, opts ...Options) error
func UnmarshalDecode(in *jsontext.Decoder, out any, opts ...Options) error

The and functions have a signature similar to , but accept options to configure their behavior. The and functions directly operate on an or , avoiding the need to temporarily construct an or just to write or read from such types. The and functions operate on a and and are actually the underlying implementation of the previously mentioned functions. Unlike , options are a first-class argument to each of the marshal and unmarshal functions, greatly extending the flexibility and configurability of . There are several options available in which are not covered by this article.

Type-specified customization

Similar to , allows types to define their own JSON representation by satisfying particular interfaces.

type Marshaler interface {
    MarshalJSON() ([]byte, error)
}
type MarshalerTo interface {
    MarshalJSONTo(*jsontext.Encoder) error
}

type Unmarshaler interface {
    UnmarshalJSON([]byte) error
}
type UnmarshalerFrom interface {
    UnmarshalJSONFrom(*jsontext.Decoder) error
}

The and interfaces are identical to those in . The new and interfaces allow a type to represent itself as JSON using a or . This allows options to be forwarded down the call stack, since options can be retrieved via the accessor method on the or .

Caller-specified customization

In , the caller of and can also specify a custom JSON representation for any arbitrary type, where caller-specified functions take precedence over type-defined methods or the default representation for a particular type.

func WithMarshalers(*Marshalers) Options

type Marshalers struct { ... }
func MarshalFunc[T any](fn func(T) ([]byte, error)) *Marshalers
func MarshalToFunc[T any](fn func(*jsontext.Encoder, T) error) *Marshalers

func WithUnmarshalers(*Unmarshalers) Options

type Unmarshalers struct { ... }
func UnmarshalFunc[T any](fn func([]byte, T) error) *Unmarshalers
func UnmarshalFromFunc[T any](fn func(*jsontext.Decoder, T) error) *Unmarshalers

While aims to behave the same as , its behavior has changed in some ways to address problems in , most notably:

  • reports an error in the presence of invalid UTF-8.

  • reports an error if a JSON object contains a duplicate name.

  • marshals a nil Go slice or Go map as an empty JSON array or JSON object, respectively.

  • unmarshals a JSON object into a Go struct using a case-sensitive match from the JSON member name to the Go field name.

  • redefines the tag option to omit a field if it would have encoded as an “empty” JSON value (which are , , , and ).

  • reports an error when trying to serialize a , which currently has no default representation, but provides options to let the caller decide.

For most behavior changes, there is a struct tag option or caller-specified option that can configure the behavior to operate under or semantics, or even other caller-determined behavior. See “Migrating to v2” for more information.

The performance of is roughly at parity with . Sometimes it is slightly faster, but other times it is slightly slower. The performance of is significantly faster than , with benchmarks demonstrating improvements of up to 10x.

In order to obtain greater performance gains, existing implementations of and should migrate to also implement and , so that they can benefit from processing JSON in a purely streaming manner. For example, recursive parsing of OpenAPI specifications in methods significantly hurt performance in a particular service of Kubernetes (see kubernetes/kube-openapi#315), while switching to improved performance by orders of magnitude.

On top of structural improvements, we’re continuing to invest in performance optimizations in the implementation for cases where the implementation is slower than . You can expect additional improvements in Go 1.28.

The Go 1 compatibility promise is a core guarantee from the Go project that allows developers to build applications that will stand the test of time and continue working on future versions of Go.

The original and new packages are of course both subject to the Go 1 compatibility promise. Applications using will continue to be supported indefinitely and need not ever migrate to .

That said, when designing the packages we wanted to do better than keeping supported. We wanted to ensure that and are compatible with one another so that packages using different versions can work together. Doing so allows a smooth ecosystem migration rather than forcing users to use one version or another due to the choices of their dependencies.

For instance, suppose your package uses to marshal a struct containing a field with a type defined in another package. That package may use the original method to define its marshaling behavior. No problem, supports methods, so marshaling will continue working as expected.

Vice versa, suppose your package uses to marshal the same struct. The other package may use the method for better performance. No problem here either, as the implementation supports ’s method under the hood.

We’ve achieved this by designing the new packages such that, under the hood, is implemented in terms of . As mentioned above, supports a variety of . Each behavior difference is controlled by one of these options. Thus, can be implemented in terms of by passing the full set of compatibility options.

With this approach, backwards-compatible additions such as new methods (e.g., ) or new struct tags (e.g., ) are automatically supported to the benefit of existing users.

Implementing in terms of options has the additional benefit of allowing gradual migration of callsites.

documents the full set of behavior differences between and , and which option controls those behaviors.

Many applications can migrate directly to with no visible behavior changes, but applications that depend on behavior can use the options to change only the behaviors they depend on.

For example, we can select all behavior except that duplicate names are allowed:

json.Marshal(..., json.DefaultOptionsV2(), jsontext.AllowDuplicateNames(true))

Alternatively, we can select all behavior except that duplicate names are disallowed:

json.Marshal(..., jsonv1.DefaultOptionsV1(), jsontext.AllowDuplicateNames(false))

For additional references on working with the new JSON packages, see:

The planning for a new major version of spanned years. In late 2020, spurred on by the inability to fix issues in the current package, Daniel Martí (one of the maintainers of ) first drafted his thoughts on what a hypothetical package should look like. Separately, after previous work on the Go API for Protocol Buffers, Joe Tsai was disappointed that the package needed to use a custom JSON implementation because was neither capable of adhering to the stricter JSON standard that the Protocol Buffer specification required, nor of efficiently serializing JSON in a streaming manner.

Believing a brighter future for JSON was both beneficial and achievable, Daniel and Joe joined forces to brainstorm on and started to build a prototype (with the initial code being a polished version of the JSON serialization logic from the Go protobuf module). Over time, a few others (Roger Peppe, Chris Hines, Johan Brandhorst-Satzkorn, Damien Neil, Austin Clements, and Michael Pratt) joined the effort by providing design review, code review, and regression testing. Many of the early discussions are publicly available in our recorded meetings and meeting notes. Later discussions are available in our working group meeting notes.

The effort took about 6 years to reach this point, incorporating feedback from many contributors and also gaining valuable empirical experience from use in production settings.

It’s worth noting that it’s largely been developed and promoted by people not employed by Google, demonstrating that the Go project is a collaborative endeavor with a thriving global community dedicated to improving the Go ecosystem.

Thank you to everyone that contributed!

items.title: Our Response To The eMudhra Key Disclosure Incident
items.author: Roland Shoemaker, on behalf of the Go Security team
items.content:
On October 19, the Go team initiated an expedited security release to protect Go users and their applications from a critical public key infrastructure (PKI) compromise involving certificates issued by eMudhra.

Within approximately seven and a half hours of being notified, we shipped a targeted patch, which was included in our first-ever URGENT track security release.

Here is the context behind the incident, why Go stepped in at the runtime level to protect our users and how our incident response unfolded.

On October 17, Mozilla added eight intermediate certificates (six used for TLS, and two used for code signing) issued by a root certificate controlled by eMudhra to OneCRL, effectively blocking their usage in Firefox. Soon after, a number of security researchers noticed this and began investigating what might’ve caused this.

On October 19, the Go Security team was made aware of these investigations and their conclusions, which showed that the keys associated with these intermediates were trivially weak, allowing recovery of the private keys in microseconds.

Due to the fact that the eMudhra root certificate was present in most trusted root programs, recovering the private keys would allow any attacker to sign arbitrary TLS certificates for any domain name, without the usual requirement to show proof of control of said domain name. This would allow an attacker to man-in-the-middle (MITM) TLS connections and present a valid certificate for a domain name they did not control, effectively allowing them to impersonate any TLS server the targeted machine attempted to connect to.

Go ships a TLS certificate verifier in the standard library. When users use or to connect to a TLS service, the verifier is called to check if the certificates the other side of the connection presents are valid. On Windows and macOS we delegate these checks to the platform APIs, and on Linux, which lacks platform APIs, we use our own verifier implementation.

Since Linux does not have a uniform built-in mechanism to handle revocation checking, and in order to provide a timely fix for users on other platforms that might not receive platform updates, we decided the best way to protect Go users was to do an URGENT track security release which similarly removed trust.

A typical Go security release follows a multi-day process, with advanced pre-announcements in order to allow those who rely on Go to prepare. In this case, because we believed that private key exposure was imminent, our team chose to use the URGENT track for the first time in order to ship protections before active public exploitation could begin.

Our Security team was alerted by an independent external researcher, citing unreported actions by Mozilla and other organizations to remove trust in eight eMudhra intermediates. It became clear quickly that this was due to weak private keys they used.

Mozilla independently reported the issue to our Security team, confirming the issue, and asking that we not immediately disclose the issue, but encouraging us to release a fix as soon as possible.

We finalized a patch which blocked the usage of certificates which chained to the compromised intermediates, and thanks to the researcher who initially alerted us to the issue, had a set of certificates signed using the recovered keys to test against.

We began the process to release minor Go versions 1.27.3 and 1.26.10 containing our patch. Due to the urgent nature of this issue and its exploitability, and with the belief that the private keys would likely become publicly known within hours, we decided an immediate release was the most prudent option.

We finalized the release and announced it publicly. At this time the underlying issue was still not widely known. In an effort to give other defenders a chance to protect as many users as possible without revealing to attackers how the issue could be exploited, our patch and communications were somewhat opaque, warning users that we were “blocking trust in a small set of intermediate certificates due to specific security concerns around their operation” and urging users to immediately upgrade to this release.

In under seven and a half hours from initial notification, patched Go releases were live worldwide, giving users everything they needed to secure their deployments before the keys became public.

By the morning of October 20, numerous independent researchers had publicly disclosed the weak keys.

Lessons Learned and Future Improvements

This was our first ever URGENT track security release, and during the release process we ran into a number of issues which caused the release to take longer than expected.

While we are happy we were able to get a release out the same day we were notified of the issue, in the modern security environment we feel that we should be able to provide releases in a more compressed timeline. The issues we ran into caused our release process to take just under four and a quarter hours from start to finish.

These issues had previously not been problematic, since the typical release process is split up over a number of days.

We’ve subsequently made a number of changes to improve our release efficiency, which should significantly reduce the time it takes us to push out a release, enhancing our ability to quickly respond to urgent security threats.

PRIVATE track security fixes are pre-announced three to seven days before their release. URGENT track fixes happen on a shorter time schedule, but we could have pre-announced the upcoming release when we began the release process, giving users at least a few hours to prepare.

While on Windows and macOS we rely on the revocation mechanisms the platform APIs provide, on Linux we don’t currently have a similar mechanism. The lack of this support was one of our major drivers to issue an expedited security release, as we did not want to leave Linux users exposed to this issue longer than was necessary.

Hence we are planning on prioritizing work to bring parity to revocation support on Linux, to help mitigate this class of issues in the future. Part of this work will involve investigating adding support for the upki project, which aims to “provide reliable, privacy-preserving and efficient certificate revocation” for Linux (see issue #82402).

Upgrading and Verifying Your Deployments

If you run Go binaries which interact with network services using TLS (such as directly via or or via a dependency such as gRPC), ensure you are running on the latest minor releases. Binaries rebuilt with Go 1.27.3 and 1.26.10 will automatically reject certificates issued by the compromised eMudhra intermediates.

You can verify your current toolchain version using and you can check the version of Go a binary was built with using go version -m <path_to_your_binary>.

The govulncheck tool can also be used to determine if a binary is affected by this issue:

$ GOTOOLCHAIN=go1.27.3+auto go install golang.org/x/vuln/cmd/govulncheck@latest
$ govulncheck -mode=binary <path_to_your_binary>

Securing Go Deployments Everywhere

For us, securing Go and its users extends beyond fixing direct security vulnerabilities in the runtime and libraries we ship. In order to keep the ecosystem secure, we believe we also need to provide users with the right tools to write secure software, look towards the future of cryptographic algorithms and protocols, and proactively respond to ecosystem wide issues when we can.

We are grateful to the independent security researchers and the Mozilla security team for this rapid notification and coordination during this incident.

items.title: Help set Go's priorities for next year
items.author: Cameron Balahan, on behalf of the Go team
items.content:
Hi Gophers! The 2026 Go Developer Survey is now open. We run this survey every year to understand how you use Go and the challenges you face. Your answers directly shape how we plan and prioritize our work.

Last year, 5,379 of you responded, and your top frustration was making sure your code follows best practices and Go idioms (33% of respondents). Since then, we shipped a rewritten in Go 1.26 that automatically modernizes your code, and added more modernizers in Go 1.27. You can read everything we learned in the 2025 results.

Take the survey here. It’s open through , takes about 10–20 minutes, and every question is optional. We’ll share the results on this blog in early 2027.

Please share the survey with your colleagues, friends, and online communities—the more Go developers we hear from, the better we understand what you need.

Thank you for helping shape the future of Go!

items.title: Interactive refactoring in gopls
items.author: Hongxiang Jiang
items.content:
When editing code in a modern IDE or editor, developers rely on its refactoring features to automate common transformations. Today, we are excited to introduce in gopls, powered by a new capability we are proposing for the Language Server Protocol (LSP) that brings dynamic, multi-step dialogs directly into your favorite editor. Crucially, we designed this capability (in collaboration with the Dart team) not just for Go, but as an open standard for all programming languages and editor ecosystems. Working support is already available in gopls v0.24.0 and the official Go extension for VS Code v0.56.0.

What is the Language Server Protocol (LSP)?

The LSP is an open standard that decouples language-specific features from specific text editors. As you navigate and edit code, your editor (such as VS Code, Neovim, or Emacs) and a language server (like gopls) engage in a continuous JSON-RPC exchange to provide features like autocomplete, hover documentation, diagnostics, and code actions.

Today, almost every code transformation in the LSP is like a function of no parameters: you trigger the operation, and the server immediately computes the edits. (Renaming a symbol is the sole exception: because it is a function of one parameter, the desired new name, it required its own dedicated RPC in the protocol.)

The language server must deduce the user’s intent from context alone, namely the cursor position and the enclosing syntax tree. When that context is not enough, the server is forced into one of two choices: apply a one-size-fits-all default, or refrain from offering the transformation altogether. The limitation lies not in gopls’s ability to compute the necessary edits, but in the LSP’s lack of a mechanism for language servers to ask the user for input.

For many transformations, this parameterless model works well. But many others need additional input from the user: which struct tags to add and in what naming convention, which interface to implement, which file to move a declaration to. Without a way to ask, gopls could only guess—“Add struct tags”, for example, always produced tags in —or not offer the refactoring at all. With interactive refactoring, language servers can now easily provide new operations with one or more parameters.

While some language extensions have worked around this limitation by embedding custom, language-specific dialog logic directly into individual editors, doing so leaves behind other editors (such as Neovim and Emacs) that stick strictly to the LSP with minimal custom client code. More importantly, editor-specific workarounds go against the fundamental purpose of the LSP: to decouple language-specific features from editors so that each server improvement benefits every client.

Interactive refactorings in action

Adding and removing struct tags (gopls v0.23.0)

When configuring serialization formats, developers frequently need custom tags and casing conventions. Previously, running “Add struct tags” unconditionally injected tags using formatting.

With interactive refactoring:

  1. Place your cursor on any struct definition and select the code action.
  2. An input dialog appears, pre-filled with , allowing you to customize any combination of tags (such as ).
  3. A second dialog lets you select your desired naming convention (such as , , or ).
  4. Gopls generates and applies the formatted struct tags across your type definition.

Here is the before-and-after transformation:

type UserProfile struct {
    ID        int64
    FirstName string
    LastName  string
    EmailAddr string
}

type UserProfile struct {
    ID        int64  `json:"id" db:"id"`
    FirstName string `json:"first_name" db:"first_name"`
    LastName  string `json:"last_name" db:"last_name"`
    EmailAddr string `json:"email_addr" db:"email_addr"`
}

Similarly, now asks you for the specific tag keys you wish to delete (for example, removing only tags while preserving the tag), rather than wiping out all struct tags indiscriminately.

Implementing interfaces with dynamic symbol search

When creating a type to satisfy an interface, developers previously had to copy the interface declaration and manually turn it into a set of methods on the receiver type (or rely on external tools like by manually typing the receiver and qualifying the name of the interface).

Since gopls v0.23.0, with interactive refactoring:

  1. Place your cursor on any concrete type and select the “Add methods to X to implement an interface…” code action.
  2. A text entry field appears, inviting you to choose the name of an interface type. It makes dynamic queries to gopls to auto-complete names of types in your workspace and the standard library (for example, ).
  3. If the selected interface has type parameters, gopls asks for a concrete type argument for each type parameter (such as ).
  4. Gopls generates complete method stubs with appropriate receiver names and instantiated method signatures.
type Foo struct{}

type MyHasher struct{}

type Foo struct{}

type MyHasher struct{}

// Equal implements [maphash.Hasher].
func (m *MyHasher) Equal(x Foo, y Foo) bool {
    panic("unimplemented")
}

// Hash implements [maphash.Hasher].
func (m *MyHasher) Hash(*maphash.Hash, Foo) {
    panic("unimplemented")
}

Moving declarations across files and packages (preview)

Moving declarations manually by cutting and pasting can easily break references and requires tedious import cleanup across multiple files. While scheduled for an upcoming gopls release, our working implementation already demonstrates how interactive file selection streamlines cross-file and cross-package moves:

  1. Place your cursor on any top-level declaration and select the code action.
  2. A file picker dialog lets you choose an existing destination file or specify a new file path.
  3. Gopls moves the declaration along with its dependent declarations (such as unexported helpers or methods) while leaving unrelated symbols in place, updates references across your workspace, and cleans up imports in both the source and destination files.

In the example below, we move the type from package to package . Its method and the unexported constant , which only uses, move along with it, while the unrelated function stays behind:

// from/from.go
package from

import (
    "fmt"
    "strings"
)

const bar = "bar"

// Doc comment for Foo
type Foo struct{}

func (f Foo) Print() {
    fmt.Println(bar)
}

func Baz() string {
    return strings.ToUpper("baz")
}

// from/from.go
package from

import "strings"

func Baz() string {
    return strings.ToUpper("baz")
}

// to/to.go
package to

import "fmt"

const bar = "bar"

// Doc comment for Foo
type Foo struct{}

func (f Foo) Print() {
    fmt.Println(bar)
}

Slaying the dragon (gopls v0.24.0)

As a demonstration of multi-step interactive dialogs and a self-contained test case for client editor implementations, gopls v0.24.0 offers a code action when you place your cursor on a package-level variable named (for example, ). Happy hunting!

Interactive refactoring establishes a foundational capability in gopls, opening up several exciting directions on our roadmap:

  • Change signature refactoring (#38028): Adding, removing, or reordering function parameters across a workspace requires input that cannot be deduced from syntax alone, such as the new parameter order or the default argument expression to insert at existing call sites. Interactive forms allow gopls to collect these details before rewriting the declaration and all call sites.
  • Interactive conflict resolution: When a code transformation encounters naming collisions, identifier shadowing, or ambiguous references, gopls can ask the user for guidance, such as asking for permission to proceed or offering to rename conflicting symbols on the fly.
  • Interactive commands beyond code edits: Because interactivity is modeled at the LSP command layer, it naturally generalizes to non-edit server operations that require user configuration, such as configuring test or benchmark runs with profiling flags (CPU, memory, tracing).

Getting Started and Sharing Feedback

Interactive refactoring is available in gopls v0.24.0 and v0.56.0 (with proof-of-concept client integrations also explored for Neovim and Emacs).

We would love to hear your thoughts as we continue refining interactive code actions in gopls:

(Special thanks to Alan Donovan, Alex Putman, Brian Wilkerson, Danny Tuppeny, Hana Kim, Madeline Kalil, Peter Weinberger, and Robert Findley for their insights, discussions, feedback, and collaboration on this work.)
